evidence.claim: Opposition BNP gatherings were regularly denied permission or confined to specific places, and police or ruling-party activists sometimes used force to disperse demonstrations; the government generally did not respect peaceful assembly.
evidence.title: 2022 Country Report on Human Rights Practices: Bangladesh
evidence.excerpt: Opposition BNP gatherings were regularly denied permission or confined to specific places, and police or ruling-party activists sometimes used force to disperse demonstrations; the government generally did not respect peaceful assembly.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Detailed 2022 reporting on repeated assembly restrictions and enforcement behavior.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the ruling government, police, and Awami League-aligned actors.
contrary_evidence: The report acknowledges the law provides a formal right to peaceful assembly and that permission was sometimes granted under conditions.

evidence.claim: The government used transnational repression and related harassment to intimidate critics abroad and relatives at home, including surveillance, reprisals, and pressure on diaspora critics and their families.
evidence.title: 2022 Country Report on Human Rights Practices: Bangladesh
evidence.excerpt: The government used transnational repression and related harassment to intimidate critics abroad and relatives at home, including surveillance, reprisals, and pressure on diaspora critics and their families.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official report with concrete examples and direct attribution to state behavior.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the Hasina government and security/police services; not necessarily to Hasina personally.
contrary_evidence: The report also notes that some critics pursued judicial remedies, though courts were often insufficiently independent.

evidence.claim: HRW said opposition groups reported an escalation of repression, including mass arrests and police raids of opposition homes, while ruling-party supporters attacked opposition meetings and authorities failed to investigate them properly.
evidence.title: Bangladesh: Crackdown on Political Opposition
evidence.excerpt: HRW said opposition groups reported an escalation of repression, including mass arrests and police raids of opposition homes, while ruling-party supporters attacked opposition meetings and authorities failed to investigate them properly.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Established rights monitor with contemporaneous reporting, named incidents, and direct quotations.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to Bangladesh authorities and ruling-party supporters under Hasina’s government.
contrary_evidence: HRW notes each side accused the other of instigating violence, so some incident-level fault remains contested.

evidence.claim: Two senior BNP leaders were arrested amid a crackdown in which at least seven people were shot dead and thousands arrested, with the BNP saying the detentions were meant to stop a planned Dhaka rally.
evidence.title: Two Bangladeshi opposition leaders arrested in government crackdown
evidence.excerpt: Two senior BNP leaders were arrested amid a crackdown in which at least seven people were shot dead and thousands arrested, with the BNP saying the detentions were meant to stop a planned Dhaka rally.
evidence.source_locator: Lead paragraph and mid-article report on arrests and casualties
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Major independent outlet citing named parties, dates, and on-the-ground claims; still journalistic rather than adjudicative.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to Hasina’s government and police actions; not a finding of personal command.
contrary_evidence: The government said arrests were on suspicion of instigating violence, so its justification was defensive rather than openly suppressive.

evidence.claim: Bangladesh’s Editors’ Council said the Digital Security Act obstructed media freedom and that journalists, activists, artists, and writers had been hit with cases under it; the article also reports the law minister acknowledged misuse.
evidence.title: Digital Security Act hinders freedom of media: Editor’s Council
evidence.excerpt: Bangladesh’s Editors’ Council said the Digital Security Act obstructed media freedom and that journalists, activists, artists, and writers had been hit with cases under it; the article also reports the law minister acknowledged misuse.
evidence.source_locator: Article body and quoted Editors’ Council statement
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Local outlet reporting a public statement by editors, with direct government acknowledgment of abuse.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the Hasina government’s legal environment and ministerial stance.
contrary_evidence: The law minister said the government would not repeal the law and framed it as cybercrime enforcement, not repression.

evidence.claim: The draft BTRC regulation would require traceability of messages, 72-hour takedowns of flagged content, data retention, and broader intermediary duties that could weaken encryption and expand state control over online speech.
evidence.title: Internet Impact Brief: Bangladesh: Regulation for Digital, Social Media and OTT Platforms, 2021
evidence.excerpt: The draft BTRC regulation would require traceability of messages, 72-hour takedowns of flagged content, data retention, and broader intermediary duties that could weaken encryption and expand state control over online speech.
evidence.source_locator: Context and numbered requirements, especially lines 73-93 and 117-124
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Technical policy analysis by a reputable internet-governance organization using the draft text directly.
evidence.period_fit: Directly covers a 2022 draft from Bangladesh regulators.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to the Hasina government’s telecom regulator and policy apparatus.
contrary_evidence: The brief notes some clauses purport to safeguard free speech and privacy, though it argues they are insufficient.

evidence.claim: RSF described Bangladesh’s state broadcasters as government propaganda outlets, said Awami League supporters often use targeted physical violence and judicial harassment against disliked ჟურნალისტs, and called the Digital Security Act one of the world’s most draconian laws for journalists.
evidence.title: Bangladesh 2022 - EN
evidence.excerpt: RSF described Bangladesh’s state broadcasters as government propaganda outlets, said Awami League supporters often use targeted physical violence and judicial harassment against disliked ჟურნალისტs, and called the Digital Security Act one of the world’s most draconian laws for journalists.
evidence.source_locator: Media landscape, political context, and legal framework sections
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Specialist press-freedom monitor with country-level analysis, though not a legal finding.
evidence.period_fit: Country analysis anchored in the 2022 period.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributes the hostile media environment to Sheikh Hasina’s government and Awami League supporters.
contrary_evidence: RSF also notes that Prothom Alo and The Daily Star retained some editorial independence, so the media space was not fully closed.

evidence.claim: The law minister said there was no scope to restore the caretaker government system because the Supreme Court had declared it illegal, rejecting the opposition’s election-time neutrality demand.
evidence.title: No scope to go back to caretaker regime: Law minister
evidence.excerpt: The law minister said there was no scope to restore the caretaker government system because the Supreme Court had declared it illegal, rejecting the opposition’s election-time neutrality demand.
evidence.source_locator: Article body and quoted ministerial remarks
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct quote from a senior government official on a core transfer-rule issue.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the Hasina government through its law minister, not to a separate institution.
contrary_evidence: The statement invokes the court and constitution, but it also concretely blocks the opposition’s preferred election-time transfer mechanism.

evidence.claim: Police were strict in denying BNP a road rally but allowed Awami League rallies with fewer constraints, and BNP was permitted to rally at Suhrawardy Udyan only on 26 conditions.
evidence.title: Awami League rallies: Police remain silent over permission, condition
evidence.excerpt: Police were strict in denying BNP a road rally but allowed Awami League rallies with fewer constraints, and BNP was permitted to rally at Suhrawardy Udyan only on 26 conditions.
evidence.source_locator: Article body describing rally permissions and contrasting treatment
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Local reporting on a specific administrative decision with clear comparative treatment.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to Dhaka police and the ruling-party environment under Hasina’s government.
contrary_evidence: The article shows some opposition permission existed, but only under heavy conditions and venue restriction.

unresolved_gaps: No direct Hasina-specific 2022 decision on nuclear safety appointments, command-and-control, or emergency doctrine.
No independent audit of Rooppur safety performance or BAERA independence in the target year.
No direct Bangladesh-initiated interstate war, proxy war, or coercive military campaign in 2022.
Direct command-chain evidence for specific 2022 abuses remains thin.
Stronger direct evidence is still needed on institutional restraint, especially courts, election administration, and oversight bodies.
Household-level distribution and independent execution evidence are thinner than macro and program-announcement evidence.
Direct ruler causation for service delivery is thinner than outcome evidence.
Direct first-person evidence of correction, admission, or disclosure is still thin.
The plot-allocation/self-dealing allegations need stronger independent corroboration or final adjudication.
Independent audits of implementation quality and outcome progress are still limited compared with announced-program evidence.
Direct evidence that Hasina personally monitored, corrected, or replaced ineffective implementers is sparse.
